Reproducibility and interval coverage

Source: vignettes/implementation.Rmd
implementation.Rmd

If you report results from bayesEfron, you may be asked whether the fit can be reproduced and what evidence there is that its intervals have their nominal coverage. Here we collect what you need to answer: how to reproduce a fit, what a fitted object stores, the two Stan programs, the checks that we ran on the computations, interval coverage in simulated data, and how the package relates to the paper (Lee and Sui 2025).

library(bayesEfron)

Our example is krw_fit, a fit that comes with the package. It is the fit to the callback gaps of 97 firms that vignette("bayesEfron") analyzes.

fit <- krw_fit

Reproducing a fit

A fitted object records what produced its draws. We first print the seed, the CmdStan version, the name of the Stan program and the first characters of a hash of the program’s file.

fit$metadata$seed
#> [1] 20250807
fit$metadata$cmdstan_version
#> [1] "2.38.0"
attr(fit$metadata, "program")
#> [1] "efron_mix"
substr(fit$metadata$stan_file_sha256, 1, 12)
#> [1] "0ea40bf867ec"

If you do not set seed in bayes_efron_fit(), the sampler’s seed is taken from the clock, and it is stored either way. Of the two Stan programs, which are described below, efron_mix is the default.

The sampler settings are stored as an attribute of metadata, and so are the bayesEfron and cmdstanr versions that made the fit.

settings <- attr(fit$metadata, "sampler_settings")
str(settings[c("chains", "iter_warmup", "iter_sampling", "adapt_delta",
               "max_treedepth", "init")])
#> List of 6
#>  $ chains       : int 4
#>  $ iter_warmup  : int 1000
#>  $ iter_sampling: int 3000
#>  $ adapt_delta  : num 0.9
#>  $ max_treedepth: int 10
#>  $ init         : num 0.5
attr(fit$metadata, "package_version")
#> [1] "0.4.0"
attr(fit$metadata, "cmdstanr_version")
#> [1] "0.8.0"

Another attribute is the grid, stored as make_efron_grid() returned it, together with the method that chose its range. By default this is "pilot", which fits the model once on a wide range before it sets the limits of the grid. Because this pilot fit runs with the seed of the call, the grid is reproduced along with the rest.

grid <- attr(fit$metadata, "grid")
grid$grid_method
#> [1] "pilot"
grid$support
#> [1] -0.08289621  0.15852607
str(grid$pilot[c("narrowed", "seed", "iter_warmup", "iter_sampling")])
#> List of 4
#>  $ narrowed     : logi FALSE
#>  $ seed         : int 20250807
#>  $ iter_warmup  : int 500
#>  $ iter_sampling: int 500

Here the pilot fit used the same seed as the fit and did not narrow the range.

Finally, fit$metadata$data_list contains the data and the spline basis. If you use the same data, settings, seed and versions on the same machine, you get the same draws. On another machine or with another CmdStan version the draws can differ, and the results then agree only to within Monte Carlo error.

Stored draws and the size of a fit

By default a fit stores the draws of the spline coefficients, lambda and \(g\), with five quantities computed from them, and nothing for the sites. Every site summary is computed from the draws of \(g\) when a method needs it, as vignette("model") describes, so the size of a fit does not grow with the number of sites.

The dimensions of the draws and the storage attribute show what the example fit contains.

dim(fit$draws)
#> [1] 200   4 114
str(attr(fit$metadata, "storage")[c("site_draws", "iterations", "chains",
                                    "thin")])
#> List of 4
#>  $ site_draws: logi FALSE
#>  $ iterations: int 200
#>  $ chains    : int 4
#>  $ thin      : int 15

We made the example fit with thin = 15, so it has 800 draws of 114 variables. Without thinning the same fit has 12,000 draws, which take about 10 megabytes. A fit made with site_draws = TRUE also stores five variables for each site, as version 0.3.0 did, and its 12,000 draws take about 55 megabytes for the 97 firms and about 697 megabytes for 1,500 sites. These sizes are for the draws alone, and the fitted object as a whole is a little larger.

Thinning only reduces what is stored. The sampler diagnostics still describe the whole run, as vignette("diagnostics") explains. You can also store the cmdstanr fit object, with keep_cmdstan_fit = TRUE, but it refers to temporary files and is only useful in the session that created it.

Fits saved by earlier versions

A fit that was saved by an earlier version of the package can still be used, although it may lack some of the attributes described above. If its table of site effects or its effective_params was computed under earlier definitions, the methods compute them again from the stored draws of \(g\) and issue a warning, and the saved object is not changed (see ?bef_fit). A saved result of summary() contains no draws, so it cannot be updated in this way: print() throws an error that asks you to call summary() again on the fit. For a fit saved by the first released version, 0.1.0, diagnose(), predict() and loo() are not available and throw an error.

Two Stan programs

bayesEfron contains two Stan programs. To read them, find the files with system.file():

system.file("stan", "efron_mix.stan", package = "bayesEfron")
system.file("stan", "efron_re.stan", package = "bayesEfron")

The default program is efron_mix.stan, and its comments state the model that vignette("model") describes. It allows a normal component at each grid point, computes the likelihood of all the sites as one matrix product, and writes nothing for the sites.

The other program, efron_re.stan, is the program of version 0.3.0. We have left it as it was, and a test in the package checks that the file has the same hash as the released one. For a \(g\) with point masses the two programs describe the same model, and a test checks that their fits of the callback data agree within Monte Carlo error.

Each program is compiled the first time it is needed, and the compiled model is stored in your user cache directory and reused in later sessions. Its file name includes a hash of the Stan file, the CmdStan version and the machine architecture, so the program is compiled again when the Stan file or the CmdStan version changes. See ?bayes_efron_compile for where the directory is and how to clear it.

Reproducing a result of version 0.3.0

To obtain a result of version 0.3.0 again, set settings = "0.3.0". The fit then runs efron_re.stan with the grid method, the 101 grid points and the site-level draws of that version:

bayes_efron_fit(raudenbush1985, seed = 1985, settings = "0.3.0")

For the same seed this gives the draws of version 0.3.0, provided that the CmdStan version, the compiler and the machine are the same as well. Another CmdStan version can change the draws, and also the number of digits with which they are written.

The current program writes its draws with 12 significant digits, and the site summaries are computed from the draws of \(g\) (see above), so estimates far from zero need no centering. In a fit with settings = "0.3.0", however, the site-level draws are written with CmdStan’s default number of digits (8 in recent versions). They lose the digits in which the sites differ when the estimates are about 10 million times their standard errors or more, so center such estimates first.

For a fit made with settings = "0.3.0", the summaries follow the definitions of the current version. To get the interval limits as version 0.3.0 computed them, use confint(method = "draws").

The data and the stored results

The vignettes use three data sets, each with a stored fit (krw_fit, twin_towers_fit and raudenbush_fit).

  • krw_discrimination contains the callback gaps of 97 firms from the experiment of Kline et al. (2022). It uses the sample of Kline et al. (2024), and we recomputed the estimates from the replication files of Walters (2024).
  • twin_towers is one simulated data set with 1,500 sites from the simulation study of Lee and Sui (2025), taken from that study’s files.
  • raudenbush1985 contains the 19 studies of Raudenbush and Bryk (1985).

A fourth data set, star_schools, has the estimated effects of small classes in the 79 schools of Tennessee’s Project STAR. The case study that analyzes it is an article on the package website, and its fit is not installed with the package.

See each data set’s help page for its source.

We made the fits with data-raw/example-fits.R in the source repository, using the defaults (with 8 spline functions for the simulated sites) and fixed seeds. The script runs each fit with all 12,000 draws and thins it to 1 draw in 15. It then compares the site intervals from the thinned draws with the intervals from all the draws, and it fails with an error if a fit has not converged or an interval limit moves by more than 2 grid spacings.

For the simulated sites we also compared the probability that a site’s effect is positive, read on the grid points (reading = "step"), between the thinned draws and all the draws. It differs by at most 0.0013.

No model is fitted when the documentation is built. The vignettes read these fits and the files in inst/examples and inst/verification, and both directories have a README that names the script that made every file.

Checks against known answers

The checks in this section are tests in the package’s test suite (tests/testthat in the source repository), so they are run again whenever the package is checked. The tests that sample need CmdStan.

The tests check the package’s computations in two steps. In the first step the model’s formulas, written out in plain R, are compared with results obtained in another way:

  • the posterior distribution of a site effect under a normal \(g\), with the conjugate normal result
  • the mean and variance of \(g\), with Gauss-Hermite quadrature
  • the posterior mode, with a numerical optimizer

In the second step the quantities that each Stan program writes are recomputed from the spline coefficients with those R formulas, and the two are compared.

With a single normal component the default program is the normal model, so another test samples from it in that case and checks that the result agrees with the normal model. For the spline basis the package calls splines::ns(grid, df = M, intercept = FALSE), and a test checks that it uses the result unchanged. If the columns of the basis and a constant column are not linearly independent, make_efron_grid() throws an error.

Other tests compare fits with deconvolveR, the implementation by Narasimhan and Efron (2020) of the empirical Bayes estimator of Efron (2016), on three simulated data sets with equal standard errors and 20, 50 and 100 sites. We do not expect the two methods to coincide, so the tests only require them to be close: the posterior means of the site effects within one standard error of the deconvolveR estimates, with a correlation of at least 0.99, and the two estimates of \(g\) for the largest data set within 0.25 in total variation distance.

These tests show that the pieces are computed correctly. They do not show that the intervals have the right coverage, which only simulated data can.

Interval coverage in simulated data

Whether 90% intervals contain the true effects 90% of the time can only be checked where the true effects are known. We fitted three sets of simulated data with the defaults, and the code below collects the stored results in one table.

verification <- function(name) {
  read.csv(system.file("verification", name, package = "bayesEfron"),
           check.names = FALSE)
}
panels <- verification("panels-methods.csv")
panels <- panels[panels$method == "bayesEfron", ]
few <- verification("few-studies.csv")
few <- few[few$method == "bayesEfron", ]
equal <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "ebnm_comparison.rds",
                             package = "bayesEfron"))$equal_se$repeated
equal <- equal[equal$method == "bayesEfron" & equal$M == 6, ]

checked <- data.frame(
  effects = c("two groups", "two groups", paste("19 studies,", few$scenario),
              "two groups, equal standard errors"),
  sites = c(panels$K, rep(19, nrow(few)), 1500),
  data_sets = c(panels$panels, few$replications, equal$panels),
  inclusion = c(panels$inclusion, few$inclusion, equal$inclusion),
  se = c(panels$inclusion_se, few$inclusion_se, equal$inclusion_se)
)
checked[c("inclusion", "se")] <- round(checked[c("inclusion", "se")], 3)
checked
#>                             effects sites data_sets inclusion    se
#> 1                        two groups   100       100     0.901 0.004
#> 2                        two groups  1500        20     0.900 0.003
#> 3       19 studies, normal, SD 0.14    19       200     0.904 0.006
#> 4       19 studies, normal, SD 0.31    19       200     0.899 0.005
#> 5              19 studies, fitted g    19       200     0.907 0.006
#> 6 two groups, equal standard errors  1500        20     0.876 0.007

In this table, inclusion is the proportion of the true effects that lie inside the 90% intervals of site_summary(), averaged over the data sets. It estimates the coverage of those intervals, and se is its Monte Carlo standard error. There are three simulation designs.

  • In rows 1 and 2, every data set has its own true effects, which we simulated from two separate groups: a third of the sites between \(-1.7\) and \(-0.7\), and two thirds between \(0.7\) and \(2.7\). These are the populations of the simulation study of Lee and Sui (2025). The standard errors are unequal, and the largest is 9 times the smallest.
  • Rows 3 to 5 are the data sets from vignette("teacher-expectancy"), which have the standard errors of the 19 studies and true effects from three distributions.
  • In row 6, the true effects of the 20 large data sets in row 2 are each estimated with a standard error of 1.

In the five rows with unequal standard errors the coverage is between 0.899 and 0.907, which is within two standard errors of 0.90 in each row. When every standard error is equal to 1, however, it is 0.876. The fits in that row converged, and we have not isolated the cause of the shortfall. See vignette("empirical-bayes") for what is known about it and what it means in practice.

We also fitted the 20 large data sets in row 2 with 8 spline functions and with settings = "0.3.0". The next table compares the three settings.

convergence <- verification("panels-convergence.csv")
data.frame(setting = convergence$setting, valid = convergence$valid,
           rhat_max = round(convergence$rhat_max, 3),
           ess_bulk_min = round(convergence$ess_bulk_min),
           treedepth_share_max = round(convergence$treedepth_share_max, 3),
           seconds = round(convergence$sampling_seconds_median),
           inclusion = round(convergence$inclusion, 3))
#>              setting valid rhat_max ess_bulk_min treedepth_share_max seconds
#> 1           defaults    20    1.009          679               0.131      36
#> 2              M = 8    20    1.004         1538               0.000      15
#> 3 settings = "0.3.0"     5    1.084           55               0.823     145
#>   inclusion
#> 1     0.900
#> 2     0.893
#> 3     0.900

Here valid counts the fits that meet three conditions: the largest R-hat over alpha, lambda and the mean and standard deviation of \(g\) is below 1.01, the smallest bulk effective sample size is at least 400, and there is no divergent transition. The next three columns give the worst case among the 20 fits, and seconds is the median sampling time.

All 20 fits with the defaults meet the three conditions. Sampling takes a median of 36 seconds, after 32 seconds for the pilot fit that sets the range. With settings = "0.3.0", 5 of the 20 fits meet them, and sampling takes 145 seconds. Sampling is fastest with 8 spline functions, but the intervals from those fits have a coverage of 0.893, more than two standard errors below 0.90. vignette("diagnostics") uses the same table to discuss what the diagnostics do and do not measure.

These simulations cover one shape of \(g\) with many sites and three shapes with few sites, two patterns of unequal standard errors, and normal errors with known standard errors. They do not cover numbers of sites other than 19, 100 and 1,500, standard errors that are themselves poorly estimated, or effects that are related to their standard errors. You can find the scripts in data-raw/benchmark/ in the source repository, and inst/verification/README.md describes the columns of the tables.

Relation to the paper

bayesEfron implements the fully Bayesian model of Lee and Sui (2025, sec. 4). The table shows how the paper’s quantities are written in the package.

Paper Package Meaning
\(\Theta_i\) \(\theta_i\) in the documentation True effect of site \(i\)
\(\hat\theta_i\), \(\sigma_i\) theta_hat, sigma Estimate and its standard error
\(\mathcal{T} = \{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\}\) grid, with L points \(\tau_j\) Grid on which \(g\) is defined
\(Q\), an \(m \times p\) matrix B, an L by M matrix Spline basis on the grid
\(\alpha\), \(\lambda\) alpha, lambda Spline coefficients and their prior precision
\(g_j\) exp(log_g) Probability of grid point \(j\)
\(\pi_{ij}\) \(w_{ij}\) in vignette("model"); not stored Posterior probability of grid point \(j\) for site \(i\), given \(\alpha\)

In three places the package’s defaults differ from the paper, and each can be changed back to the paper’s choice.

  1. In the code of the paper’s application, the grid covers the range of the estimates extended by half its width on each side, which is grid_method = "paper_realdata". The default method, "pilot", starts from that range and narrows it where the pilot fit shows that \(g\) occupies only a part of it, but it never widens it. See vignette("choosing-a-grid") for details.
  2. The number of grid points is 101 unless the smallest standard error or the spread of the estimates is small compared with the grid spacing, in which case more points are used. Set L = 101 to keep 101 points.
  3. The paper obtains the site intervals as quantiles of posterior draws of the effects (its Appendix B.4), and so did version 0.3.0 of the package. We now compute them from the posterior distribution itself, with the probability of each grid point spread over its grid cell. In site_summary(), reading = "step" leaves the probabilities on the points, and a fit made with site_draws = TRUE gives the intervals from draws with confint(method = "draws").

To restore the first two at once, use settings = "0.3.0", which also stores the site-level draws. The other two grid methods, "paper_simulation" and "paper_sensitivity", are the methods that the code accompanying the paper, https://github.com/joonho112/fully-bayes-efron-prior, uses for its simulation study and its sensitivity analysis. Where the paper’s text and its code differ in a detail, the package follows the code. For example, the paper’s Stan appendix shows a grid that extends 0.5 units beyond the estimates on each side, whereas the simulation code builds the grid from the true effects.

confint() can also return the shortest interval with posterior probability level (interval = "hpd"). For point masses it is the shortest interval after the probability of each grid point has been spread evenly over one grid spacing around it, and where a range of intervals is equally short, the middle one is returned. For normal components the limits are moved until no nearby interval with that probability is shorter, and the length of the result is within one hundredth of the length of the shortest interval. In both cases the interval has probability level exactly. With method = "draws", and always for type = "g", it is the shortest interval that contains at least that proportion of the draws.

The package also has features that are not in the paper:

  • the normal components
  • the "pilot" method for the range, and what diagnose() reports about the grid
  • the effective number of parameters
  • the log likelihood of each site and the cross-validation built on it
  • predict()
  • the plots

The table of site effects follows the paper’s definitions (Lee and Sui 2025, sec. 4.3 and Appendix A): the posterior mean, the posterior standard deviation with both parts of the variance, the posterior mode on the grid, and an interval of the stated probability, which the package takes with equal tails.

To cite the package, please cite the paper. You can get the reference with citation("bayesEfron").

Kline, Patrick, Evan K. Rose, and Christopher R. Walters. 2024. “A Discrimination Report Card.” American Economic Review 114 (8): 2472–525. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230700.
Lee, JoonHo, and Daihe Sui. 2025. “Fully Bayesian Inference for Meta-Analytic Deconvolution Using Efron’s Log-Spline Prior.” Mathematics 13 (16): 2639. https://doi.org/10.3390/math13162639.
Narasimhan, Balasubramanian, and Bradley Efron. 2020. “deconvolveR: A G-Modeling Program for Deconvolution and Empirical Bayes Estimation.” Journal of Statistical Software 94 (11): 1–20. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v094.i11.
